title: Coordinate-free finite functional calculus
subtitle: G2 lecture 032000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded companion deck developed from the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix. Adds explicit mathematical formulas, worked examples, and topic-specific diagrams while remaining standalone.

slides.title: Turning functions into operators
slides.lead: Once a self-adjoint matrix is spectrally decomposed, any scalar function f can act on its eigenvalues.
body: The finite functional calculus packages this idea without tying it to one diagonalizing basis. If A has eigenspace projections P_λ, then f(A) should scale each λ-eigenspace by the scalar f(λ).
This single construction explains spectral projections, square roots, matrix exponentials, and many later operator functions as instances of the same mechanism.
slides.takeaway: Functional calculus means applying a scalar rule to each spectral component of A.

slides.title: Begin with one eigenvector
slides.lead: If A v = λ v, the natural requirement is that f(A) should send v to f(λ) v.
slides.mathtex: A v = \lambda v\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(A)v = f(\lambda) v
body: This requirement says the new operator keeps the same eigendirections but changes the scale attached to each eigenspace. For indicator functions we recover spectral projections, while for f(t)=t we recover A itself.
The challenge is to define f(A) on the whole space in a way that does not depend on the accidental choice of an eigenbasis inside repeated eigenspaces.
slides.takeaway: The calculus is determined by how it acts on spectral pieces, not on coordinates.

slides.title: Spectral projections give the formula
slides.lead: The orthogonal projections onto eigenspaces let us write the operator directly.
body: Each P_λ extracts the λ-eigenspace component of a vector, and the coefficient f(λ) rescales that component. Summing over the distinct eigenvalues reassembles the result.
Because the projections depend only on the operator, not on a diagonalizing basis, the formula is coordinate-free even though it is motivated by diagonalization.
slides.takeaway: Spectral projections are the stable scaffolding for finite functional calculus.

slides.title: A concrete two-dimensional calculation
slides.lead: For A = [[2,1],[1,2]] with eigenvalues 3 and 1, apply f(t)=t².
body: Diagonalizing A gives the same answer, but the projector formula avoids carrying the basis change explicitly through every computation. The result equals A², as it must when f(t)=t².
Choosing instead f = 1_(2,∞) would return P_3, and choosing f(t)=\sqrt t would return the positive square root once the eigenvalues are nonnegative.
slides.takeaway: Different functions produce different operators from the same spectral decomposition.

slides.title: Why the algebra works
slides.lead: Orthogonality of the spectral projections makes the calculus behave like ordinary pointwise algebra.
body: The key relation is P_λ P_μ = 0 when λ ≠ μ, while P_λ² = P_λ. Expanding products and collecting terms reproduces the pointwise products f(λ)g(λ).
Hence polynomial identities become operator identities after evaluation at A. This is why the functional calculus is so powerful: it preserves the algebraic structure of functions.
slides.takeaway: Pointwise algebra on the spectrum becomes operator algebra through orthogonal projections.

slides.title: Polynomial interpolation explains uniqueness
slides.lead: On a finite spectrum, many functions agree because only their values on finitely many eigenvalues matter.
body: If the distinct eigenvalues are λ₁, …, λ_k, then Lagrange interpolation produces a polynomial p with p(λ_i)=f(λ_i) for every i. Consequently p(A) already equals f(A).
This shows that the functional calculus is uniquely determined by the spectral values alone. Two scalar functions that agree on σ(A) produce exactly the same operator.
slides.takeaway: In finite dimensions, the functional calculus depends only on the values of f on the finite spectrum.

slides.title: Coordinate-free does not mean basis-free proofs are impossible
slides.lead: A diagonalizing basis is still useful for proofs and calculations, but it is not part of the final definition.
body: One may compute f(A) by diagonalizing A, applying f to the diagonal entries, and conjugating back. The projector formula proves that the result is independent of the chosen orthonormal basis inside repeated eigenspaces.
So “coordinate-free” means the operator itself is intrinsic, even if coordinates are temporarily introduced along the way.
slides.takeaway: Coordinates are a tool for derivation, not part of the mathematical object being defined.

slides.title: A function can reveal a property of A
slides.lead: Functional calculus is useful because carefully chosen functions expose structure.
body: Take f(t)=1_{[0,∞)}(t): then f(A) is the spectral projection onto the nonnegative spectral subspace. Take f(t)=|t|: then f(A) gives the modulus of a self-adjoint operator. Take f(t)=\sqrt t on [0,∞): then f(A) gives the positive square root of a positive operator.
In each case, one scalar function packages an entire operator-theoretic construction.
slides.takeaway: Useful operator constructions often amount to choosing the right scalar function.

slides.title: What changes in infinite dimensions
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 032000 · Preview of the spectral theorem
slides.lead: The finite formula is only the first case of a much broader theory.
body: For a general self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space, the spectrum need not be a finite list of eigenvalues, and there may be no eigenbasis at all. Then one replaces the finite sum by an integral against a projection-valued measure.
The finite-dimensional lecture remains essential because the same conceptual roles survive: spectral pieces, scalar functions, and reassembly into an operator.
slides.takeaway: Finite functional calculus is the discrete model of the general spectral calculus.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.lead: Rebuild the whole construction from spectral projections alone.
body: Take the finite spectral decomposition of A, replace each eigenvalue λ by f(λ), and keep the same orthogonal projections P_λ. The resulting operator is f(A). It respects sums, products, and adjoints because the spectral projections are mutually orthogonal idempotents.
That perspective unifies spectral selectors, square roots, and later exponentials under one piece of mathematics.
slides.takeaway: The finite functional calculus is the template for many later operator constructions.
